query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of Nb (about 1–2 atomic percent) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of fine, stable Nb-rich precipitates along the lamellar interfaces, thereby enhancing strength, long-term creep resistance under room-temperature conditions, and corrosion stability without significantly reducing ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure
generation.intervention: Micro-alloying by introducing approximately 1–2 at.% Nb into the alloy during melting and standard thermomechanical processing
generation.conditions: The Nb modification is performed during the standard processing route used for the baseline alloy. Afterwards, the modified alloy is tested under aerospace-relevant environmental conditions including cyclic temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading for creep at room temperature, and standardized corrosion testing environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and distribution of fine, Nb-rich nano-precipitates concentrated along the lamellar boundaries
generation.mechanism: The Nb atoms segregate at lamellar interfaces during solidification and subsequent heat treatments, leading to the nucleation of stable precipitates. These precipitates impede dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, which are mechanisms central to yield strength and creep resistance. In addition, the stabilized interface may reduce localized corrosion, enhancing the alloy’s resistance under aggressive environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in yield strength and room-temperature creep resistance with maintained or slightly enhanced ductility relative to the baseline alloy
generation.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy without Nb addition
generation.boundary: The intervention is limited to a Nb addition of approximately 1–2 at.% and assumes the same melting and thermomechanical processing conditions; improvements are expected under the test conditions reflective of aerospace applications.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the strength increase, creep resistance improvement, and any potential trade-offs with ductility are uncertain and will depend on the kinetics of precipitate formation and distribution in the modified alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set with the conventional AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and another set with an additional 1–2 at.% Nb. Process both sets under identical melting and thermomechanical conditions. Subject the samples to cyclic temperature variations representative of aerospace conditions, long-term room-temperature creep tests, and standard corrosion tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-modified alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in yield strength and creep resistance over the baseline or if its ductility is notably compromised, then the hypothesis is falsified.
